The 5G revolution promised driverless utopia, but users mostly just streamed videos—now the 6G hype train is already leaving the station.
Evidence: Telco marketing claims, researcher critiques, ACMA spectrum sales
#Tech #Telecom 🌐

Telecom leaders and regulators pitch 6G as the next great leap in connectivity, promising revolutionary speeds and seamless immersive tech by 2030.
Stated Judgement: (+0.60, +0.50) — Greater Good

Past generation leaps delivered mostly incremental speeds while locking consumers into costly spectrum auctions and recurring upgrade cycles.
Resulting Judgement: (-0.20, -0.40) — Greater Evil

Verdict: FAIL — Fall into Destruction.
Routine commercial hype meets incremental technical reality without systemic catastrophe.

Integrity: Conditionally Sound (Hypocrisy: 1.8, z: 1)

- Telecom Carriers: PASS (0.2, -0.3) — Sells incremental tech updates as revolutions.
- Regulators: PASS (0.0, -0.2) — Allocates spectrum with moderate oversight.
As 5G settles into ordinary streaming use, Australian regulators and telecom giants are already hashing out airwave rules for 6G networks arriving around 2030.

The Bright Side:
Early stakeholder friction allows regulators to address regional connectivity and spectrum costs before commercial rollouts begin.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
Confusing marketing promises (WHAT) with tangible infrastructure delivery (HOW).

Social Physics Analysis:
Carriers run a mild commercial extraction loop, using futuristic hype pretexts to secure high-value spectrum assets ahead of actual demand.

The Trajectory: The Path of Fall into Destruction.
Incremental reality grounds overhyped technical ambitions into manageable commercial cycles.

The Unavoidable Truth: New wireless generations always oversell revolutionary utility.
The Unavoidable Lie: Every upgrade solves structural digital divides.

Alethekanon:
Marketing visions routinely outpace physical infrastructure, but commercial iteration moves forward regardless.

Awwthekanon:
It's okay to just want a reliable phone that calls home without needing holographic flying cars.

Brothekanon:
They're already selling 6G when half the time my 5G drops out in the basement? Classic.

Spirithekanon:
"He who multiplies words lacks sense, but he who restrains his lips is prudent." Proverbs 10:19 FAIL
Quiet realism outweighs grand technological boasts.

Oulu, Finland: 5G was sold as the network for cloud gaming and driverless cars. More than half the phones in Australian pockets are now on 5G plans, and most of their users use them to stream the footy and send photos of the kids, much as they did on 4G.

Now the industry is preparing to sell the next generation, with the first 6G phones due around 2030.

Today’s technology has arguably failed to live up to expectations, both for consumers who were promised the future and for telcos banking on lucrative new revenue streams.

The founder of the world’s first 6G research programme, at the University of Oulu in northern Finland, has a one-line verdict on what 5G delivered: “For consumers, data transfer speeds are somewhat faster than in 4G, but that’s kind of it,” Matti Latva-aho says.

At the same university, radio engineering professor Marko Leinonen showed us an early 5G radio head built for 28-gigahertz spectrum. It was made for millimetre-wave 5G, the ultra-fast but short-range version that carriers in the US, South Korea and Japan rolled out first.

The signal barely travelled, so it needed far more towers than carriers built, and customers never trusted the coverage. “Those were not gold mines,” Leinonen says.

Australia bought into the same idea. Carriers paid for similar spectrum at auction in 2021. The Australian Communications and Media Authority, which ran the sale, now finds rollout of those networks has been more limited and gradual than expected, here and overseas.

Long before anyone can buy a 6G phone, the battle lines are already being drawn. The ACMA and the federal government must decide how much spectrum carriers can receive, what it will cost them and whether regional Australia is outsourced to offshore satellites.

As consumer group Australian Communications Action Network (ACAN) notes, these decisions will shape Australian connectivity well into the 2040s.
